opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because time is really the scarcest resource you have, whether you're a student, a professor, or building something in industry.

For me, a few things matter. The first is whether the problem is real, meaning someone actually feels the pain. A lot of my work came from that. When I was working on machine learning, I kept running into the same frustration: the models were interesting, but the tools to run them efficiently and at scale just weren't there. That pain was a strong signal. If I'm frustrated, there's a good chance many other people are too.

The second is whether there's leverage, whether solving the problem once can unlock things for many people. I've always been drawn to systems and infrastructure for that reason. If you build a good library or a compiler stack, you aren't solving one problem, you're giving thousands of people the ability to solve their own problems faster. That multiplier effect is very motivating to me.

The third is timing. Some problems are important but the moment isn't right. The hardware isn't there, or the community isn't ready. Other times you can sense a shift coming, like new kinds of models or new kinds of hardware, and there's a window where the old approaches break down. Those windows are where I think a small group can have outsized impact, because everyone is starting from roughly the same place.

And finally, honestly, I have to enjoy it. Good problems usually take years, not months. There will be long stretches where things don't work, where the benchmarks look bad and nobody is using what you built. If I don't find the problem genuinely fun to think about, it's very hard to sustain that. So I try to pick things where even the struggle feels interesting.

I'd also say you don't always know in advance. Sometimes you start with something small, a side project, and it grows because people find it useful. So I try to stay open, build things, put them out there, and listen to how people respond. The feedback often tells you which problems are really worth your time.

r001.rationale: The response says time is scarce, but does not state that a mediocre problem takes roughly as long to work on as an important one.

r002.rationale: It frames time as the scarcest resource and says he chooses problems he finds genuinely fun to sustain effort on, linking limited time to prioritizing work he wants to do.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I come back to all the time, and honestly the answer has changed as I've gone from being a student to running a lab and building things in the open.

The first filter for me is whether the problem sits at an intersection. The projects I've been most happy with, XGBoost, TVM, MLC, all came from noticing that two communities were not talking to each other. Machine learning people cared about the model, systems people cared about the hardware, and nobody owned the gap. When you find a gap like that, you get a lot of leverage, because the work is not incremental on either side. It's new to both.

The second filter is whether it will matter in a few years, not just now. I try to ask: if this works, who uses it, and does the need grow or shrink? When we started on compilers for deep learning, GPUs were dominant and some people thought that was the end of the story. But it was clear that there would be more kinds of hardware, more kinds of models, and that the cost of hand-tuning everything would explode. Betting on that direction turned out well. So I look for problems where the pain is going to get worse, not better.

The third thing, and this one is more personal, is whether I can build something concrete. I'm an engineer at heart. I like problems where there's an artifact at the end, a piece of software someone can run, rather than only a paper. Building forces you to be honest. You can't hide behind assumptions when real users file issues. And open source gives you a feedback loop that tells you very quickly whether the problem was real.

Then there's the practical side. I ask whether I have an unfair advantage. Sometimes a problem is important but someone else is better positioned, and that's fine. I'd rather pick something where my background in both ML and systems actually gives me a different angle.

Finally, I've learned to say no to things that are only interesting. Interesting is cheap. There are far more interesting problems than there is time, so the ones that win are the ones that are interesting and useful and where I believe the timing is right. If it's early, I might keep it as a side exploration. If it's late, I let it go.

And I'll admit I still get it wrong. Some things I thought would be big didn't go anywhere. But as long as the process makes me learn something I can reuse, that's not wasted time. Most of the good ideas I've had came from the leftovers of things that didn't work.

r001.rationale: The response says there are more interesting problems than available time, but does not compare the time required for mediocre and important problems.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says time is limited and uses that scarcity to explain choosing problems that are interesting, useful, and well-timed.

astra-6.text:
For me, it usually starts with a concrete bottleneck. You’re trying to build something, and you realize that the existing tools make it much harder than it should be. Then the question is: Is this just a problem for my particular application, or is there something more general underneath it?

I’m especially interested when solving that problem could enable other people to do things they couldn’t do before. You might start with one use case, but the solution becomes a building block for many different ideas.

Of course, you don’t know that at the beginning. So I like to start small, build something, and get feedback. Does it actually help? Do people use it in ways you didn’t expect? That gives you a much better signal about whether it’s worth spending the next few years on.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the time required for mediocre problems with that for important problems.

r002.rationale: It discusses deciding whether a problem is worth spending years on, but does not cite limited time as a reason to prioritize work Tianqi wants to do.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with asking whether the problem matters to people, and whether solving it could enable something beyond that one solution. I’m especially interested in problems where you can build something, learn from how people use it, and then refine your understanding.

I also ask, why now? Is there something changing that makes an old problem worth revisiting? And can I find a small, concrete starting point? You don’t always know at the beginning whether a direction will work. But if the problem is meaningful and each step teaches you something, that’s usually a good reason to spend time on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses meaningful problems but does not state that mediocre and important problems take roughly the same time.

r002.rationale: It mentions choosing where to spend time, but does not cite limited time as the reason Tianqi prioritizes work he wants to do.
